lines.caption: On November 20th, 2026, the number theorist Levent Alpöge, who works at Anthropic, posted a short note.
He says he believes that he and Claude, Anthropic's AI, have proved the Riemann Hypothesis and a broader version. He released it only as Lean code, which computers can check.
Here's what that means, and what's been checked.
Start with the primes. Two, three, five, seven, eleven.
Count them up to any number x, and you get a staircase. A smooth curve tracks it closely.
Up to a trillion there are about 37.6 billion primes, and the curve misses by only about thirty-eight thousand.
Does the fit stay that tight forever?
In 1859, Bernhard Riemann tied that question to one function, called zeta.
It's built from the whole numbers, and it encodes the primes exactly.
It has infinitely many zeros in a narrow strip of the complex plane. Riemann guessed they all sit on the strip's center line.
Computers have checked trillions. All on the line. But checking trillions isn't proving it for every one.
Each zero adds a wave, and the waves together rebuild the prime staircase.
The farther a zero sits to the right of the line, the louder its wave grows.
All on the line means no wave drowns out the rest, and the error stays near the square root of x.
The generalized version says the same for primes in patterns, like primes ending in 7.
There's a parallel world where this is already a theorem: polynomials over finite fields, where the question becomes counting points on curves.
André Weil proved it there in the 1940s. Pierre Deligne went much further in 1974.
And in 1969, Sergei Stepanov found an unusually elementary proof for certain curves.
Stepanov's trick: build a helper polynomial that's zero at every point you want to count.
Not just zero, but zero many times over.
A polynomial of limited degree can only have so many roots, counted with multiplicity. So more multiplicity means a tighter count.
And multiplicity comes from derivatives.
That's where the integers push back.
You can differentiate a polynomial. Differentiate the number seven and you just get zero.
Alpöge names exactly this gap.
His note describes a way around it.
A theta lift carries a highly symmetric object from one group of symmetries to another.
According to the note, each lift mimics one more order of multiplicity. Chain them into a ladder, and every rung buys one more.
For a sum over primes up to X, he says Claude suggested about the square root of X rungs.
Alpöge says that line alone should make mathematicians fall out of their chairs.
He says the ladder grew out of a toy: his new, unpublished proof of Weil's theorem that uses nothing but signs.
Early readers on the Lean forum report they can't find that toy in the released code.
What can be read so far is the ending. A classical argument of Landau's turns a one-sided bound on a smoothed prime count into a ban on zeros right of the line. Symmetry covers the left.
What he posted: seventeen million lines of Lean, in 175,000 files, without a single comment.
At the top, five short theorems. One states the Riemann Hypothesis exactly as Lean's shared math library defines it.
In the code, the generalized version comes first. The original falls out as a corollary.
A text search of the code finds no declared shortcuts: no unfinished steps, no added axioms.

scenes.title: The checks, and the note's timeline

lines.caption: Within hours, others were checking.

As of the evening of November 20th, independent checks report that every file compiles, the main theorems rest only on Lean's three standard axioms, and at least six independent proof checkers accept the whole proof.
One last official comparison run is expected to finish over the weekend.
The note's timeline runs from October 6th to November 16th. Alpöge says he supplied the guiding idea, and that Claude far outpaced him near the finish.
What's still missing is an explanation people can follow. No human-readable proof has been released, and Alpöge expects the argument to shrink a lot.
Three takeaways.
The Riemann Hypothesis is about how regular the primes are.
The note's key idea is a stand-in for derivatives of whole numbers.
And if it holds up, this may be one of the first major proofs a machine checked before anyone could fully explain it.
